summary: For ages 8–10, teach that two things changing together (correlation) does not prove one causes the other. Learners practise resisting the causal leap, proposing an alternative explanation (a hidden common cause, coincidence, or reversed causal direction), and recognising that a controlled/fair test — changing one variable while holding everything else constant — is what the curriculum treats as establishing cause. The anchor example is ice-cream sales and drowning (or sunburn) both rising in hot weather, with temperature as the hidden common cause.
misconceptions: Assuming that because two things rise and fall together, one must cause the other.
Never considering a hidden third factor that drives both variables.
Ignoring the possibility that the causal arrow runs the other way.
Treating a strong or striking correlation as automatically causal.
Thinking observation of a pattern alone (without a controlled test) can prove causation.
Believing coincidental correlations can't happen in 'real' data.

activities.title: Bust a fake cause by manipulating a system
steps: Watch two variables — ICE-CREAM SALES and DROWNING ACCIDENTS — plotted side by side as you scrub a month-slider; notice both lines rise together through summer and fall together in winter.
State the tempting but wrong conclusion the data invites ('it looks like ice cream causes drowning').
Reveal a hidden covered slider; find it is TEMPERATURE, then drag it and observe BOTH lines move together because of it.
Switch to CONTROL mode: pin temperature at a fixed value, then raise and lower ice-cream sales on their own, and watch whether the drowning line follows or stays flat.
Optionally switch to a scatter-plot view and watch how holding the hidden factor (temperature) fixed flattens the apparent trend between ice-cream sales and drowning.
Optionally draw or view the common-cause diagram — temperature → ice-cream sales and temperature → drowning — and contrast it with what a true direct cause (ice cream → drowning) would look like.
Explain in your own words why the flat drowning line shows that, in this model, ice cream is not what causes drowning.
Try a reversed-direction case (where B actually causes A) and a pure-coincidence case, and decide which escape route explains each.
activities.insight: A correlation can be produced by a hidden common cause, a reversed causal direction, or coincidence; holding the hidden factor fixed and changing only one variable is what tests whether a true cause exists.

activities.title: Name the confounder or the test that settles it
steps: For a given vivid correlation (ice cream / drowning, shoe size / reading age), decide whether it shows that A causes B or whether something else could explain the link.
Sort a set of claims into 'correlation only' versus 'evidence of a real cause'.
Match each correlation to its most likely explanation: a hidden common cause, a reversed direction, or coincidence.
For each case, describe a fair test, or explain why one is hard or impossible (for example, you cannot change someone's shoe size), that would help check whether A really causes B.
activities.insight: Recognising the causal leap and being able to name a plausible confounder (or the test that would decide) is distinct from merely sensing a claim is wrong.

activities.title: Interrogate a bold causal headline
steps: Read a bold causal claim (e.g. 'children with bigger feet are better at spelling — so big feet cause good spelling').
Ask probing questions out loud or in writing: Could something else cause both? Which way does the arrow point? Could this be coincidence?
Propose a hidden common cause (e.g. older/bigger children have both larger feet and more spelling practice).
Describe how you would actually test whether ice cream affects sunburn so the weather can't fool you.
State what it would take to convince you that A really causes B, not just goes with it.
activities.insight: Challenging a causal claim means actively testing it against the three escape routes — common cause, reversed direction, coincidence — and insisting on a controlled test before accepting cause.

checkQuestion: Someone notices that on days when more ice creams are sold, more people get sunburnt. They say 'eating ice cream must cause sunburn.' Do you agree? Explain what you think is really going on.
checkAnswer: Strong reasoning rejects the causal claim and identifies a third factor — hot, sunny weather — driving both ice-cream sales and sunburn, so the two rise together without one causing the other. It articulates that things happening together (correlation) does not by itself mean one causes the other, and that you would need to rule out other explanations before claiming cause.
